title: How to Write a Software Engineer Resume That Gets Past ATS
seoTitle: Software Engineer Resume That Gets Past ATS
excerpt: Applicant tracking systems read your resume before a human does. Here is how to format a software engineer resume so the software can read it, without designing for robots instead of people.
content:
Quick answer: An applicant tracking system (ATS) is the software many employers use to collect and filter job applications. To get past it, use a simple single-column layout, standard section headings, real text (not text inside images), and a plain font. Match the words in the job posting, name your skills explicitly, and avoid tables, graphics and unusual formatting that trip apps up. A resume built this way reads cleanly to both the software and the recruiter.

Most software engineering roles at larger companies are filled through an online portal, and that portal is often an applicant tracking system. You never see it, but it decides whether a person ever opens your file. The good news is that writing for it is not a trick: the resume that an ATS reads cleanly is also the one a busy recruiter can skim in ten seconds. This guide explains what the software needs and turns it into a checklist you can apply today.

What is an applicant tracking system?

An applicant tracking system is software that receives job applications, stores them, and helps a hiring team sort and search them. Recruiters use it to filter by keyword, keep notes, and move candidates through stages. It does not usually reject you on its own; in most setups a human still decides, but the ATS decides what the human sees first. If your resume is parsed badly, you may be filtered out or looked over before anyone reads it.

That distinction matters. You are not trying to beat a robot. You are trying to make sure the robot presents you accurately, so the person searching for a Python developer can actually find you.

Why does formatting matter so much?

An ATS reads your resume by converting it into plain text and trying to place each piece under the right heading. Anything that breaks that conversion loses information. Two-column layouts, text boxes, tables, headers and footers, and graphics can scramble the order or drop content entirely. A job title trapped inside an image is invisible to the parser.

Harvard's Mignone Center for Career Success tells students to tailor each resume to the role and to start from a simple, clean template rather than an elaborate design. The practical takeaway is to treat your resume as text first and a design second.

What should the layout look like?

Use a single column, top to bottom, with a clear order: contact details, then a short summary or skills block, then experience, then education, then projects or certifications. Standard headings such as Experience, Education and Skills help the parser match your content to the right fields. Use a standard, web-safe font such as Arial or Calibri, a normal body size, and save as PDF unless the posting asks for Word.

Avoid putting important text in a header, footer or sidebar, because some systems ignore those areas. Skip photos, icons and rating bars for skills; they add nothing a parser can read and can distract a human. Keep dates in a consistent format and put them against each role rather than in a separate column.

How do you use keywords without gaming the system?

Reread the job posting and note the skills it names: languages, frameworks, tools, and the kind of work. Use those exact terms where they honestly describe what you did. If the posting says "JavaScript" and "React" and you built a React app, write JavaScript and React, not "front-end wizardry." The ATS and the recruiter are both searching for the words the employer chose.

Mirror the posting's language, not its flattery. If the description calls it "continuous integration," use that phrase somewhere true in your experience. Do not stuff a hidden keyword list at the bottom or write in white text; modern systems detect it, and a human will see it, and both will count it against you.

How should you describe your experience?

Write each role with a short line on what you owned, then two to four bullets on what you did and the result. Start each bullet with a strong verb: built, shipped, migrated, reduced, designed. Where you can, add a measurable outcome, such as a percentage faster, a number of users, or a reduction in incidents. Numbers are what a recruiter's eye stops on.

Tie the work to the role you want. If you are applying for a backend role, lead with the API and database work and put the front-end detail later. Tailoring is the single highest-value effort you can make, and it is the same advice career centres give to every candidate.

What are the most common ATS mistakes?

Six mistakes cause most of the damage.

  • Using a multi-column or graphic-heavy template that scrambles the text order.
  • Putting contact details or the job title only inside a header, image or text box.
  • Listing a skill as a logo or icon that the parser cannot read.
  • Using creative job titles that hide the real one, so the keyword search misses you.
  • Leaving off exact technology names the posting uses.
  • Sending the same generic resume to every role with no tailoring.

How do you describe results with numbers?

The fastest way to make a software resume memorable is to attach an outcome to each strong bullet. "Migrated the payments service to a new database" is fine; "migrated the payments service to a new database, cutting page load from 2.1 seconds to 0.8" is better. Aim for one measurable result in your two or three most important roles, and skip numbers on minor tasks where you would be inventing them.

If you do not track metrics, describe the scale instead: the size of the user base, the number of services, the size of the team, or the volume of data. Scale tells a recruiter the difference between a hobby project and a production system, which is exactly the judgement they are trying to make quickly.

Does a cover letter help with an ATS?

Sometimes. If the application asks for one, write a short letter of three or four paragraphs that names the role, says why you fit its main requirement, and gives one concrete example. Upload it as text, not as an image, so it is stored and searchable like the resume. If the portal makes a cover letter optional and you have nothing specific to add, a strong tailored resume is worth more than a generic letter.

Should you use the same resume for every job?

No. A single tailored resume beats ten generic ones. Keep a master document with everything you have done, then for each application cut it down to the most relevant experience and adopt the posting's key terms. This keeps you honest about your history while making sure the right words appear for the role in front of you.

Do you still need to design for humans?

Yes, and this is where a lot of ATS advice goes wrong. The resume that survives the software still has to impress the person who finally reads it. Clear structure, short bullets and real results serve both readers. A plain resume with strong, specific content beats a beautiful one that parses badly, and it beats a keyword-stuffed one that reads like a robot wrote it.

Frequently asked questions

Do all companies use an ATS?

Many mid-size and large employers do, and smaller companies increasingly do too. You cannot tell from the outside, so writing a clean, parseable resume is always the safer choice.

Will an ATS reject my resume automatically?

Usually not on its own. The system mostly stores and ranks applications for recruiters, who make the decision. A badly formatted resume can still be filtered or looked over because the software read it wrong.

Should my resume be one page or two?

One page is the default for early-career engineers. Two pages is fine when you have several years of relevant experience worth showing; the rule is relevance, not a hard page limit.

What file format is best for an ATS?

A standard PDF is usually safest, and Word if the posting asks for it. Avoid scanned images and unusual formats, since the parser needs real text.

Do keywords really matter that much?

Yes, because recruiters search applications by keyword. Using the posting's own terms for skills you genuinely have makes you findable; stuffing keywords you do not have does not.

This article offers general job-search guidance. It is not a guarantee of any application outcome.
